title: Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation
answer: Protein structure, new molecules, simulated trials, toxicity forecasting and repurposing.

children.name: Protein Structure Prediction
children.blurb: Protein structure prediction estimates the three-dimensional shape of a protein from its amino acid sequence.

children.name: Designing New Molecules
children.blurb: Designing new molecules with AI covers computational generation and evaluation of candidate drug molecules, including small molecules, peptides, and antibodies.

children.name: Simulated Clinical Trials
children.blurb: Simulated clinical trials use computational models to predict how a drug or device would perform in a human population before, or instead of, running a full physical trial.

children.name: Toxicity Forecasting
children.blurb: Toxicity forecasting covers computational prediction of whether a candidate molecule will cause harm in a living system, including organ damage, mutagenicity, cardiotoxicity, and developmental or reproductive effects.

children.name: Drug Repurposing
children.blurb: Drug repurposing uses AI to find new therapeutic uses for existing approved or investigational drugs.

sections.body: Drug discovery and molecular simulation applies machine learning to the early stages of medicine development. Right now, protein structure prediction tools turn amino acid sequences into three dimensional shapes, generative models propose new chemical structures, and classifiers estimate whether a compound will be toxic. Simulated clinical trials use existing patient data to model how a drug might behave in a group, while drug repurposing compares known drugs against new disease targets. These systems produce ranked lists and predicted values that chemists and pharmacologists then test in laboratories and real trials.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most mature area is protein structure prediction, where accuracy for many single chain proteins is now high enough to guide experiments, though flexible regions and multi protein complexes remain difficult. Molecule design can generate plausible compounds, but most candidates still fail later in synthesis or animal testing. Toxicity forecasting catches some obvious hazards, yet it misses rare or long term effects because training data is limited and biased toward known compounds. Simulated trials are useful for planning, not for proving safety or efficacy, and their results can drift when patient populations differ from the training data. No part of this section replaces physical experiments or regulatory review.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking for how AI predicts shapes would start with Protein Structure Prediction, which explains the inputs, outputs, and confidence measures for folded proteins. Designing New Molecules covers the generative and search methods that propose compounds, and it pairs naturally with Toxicity Forecasting, where those proposals are screened for likely harm. Simulated Clinical Trials sits between early discovery and human testing, showing how models estimate outcomes before a real trial begins. Drug Repurposing is the most applied page, describing how existing approved drugs are matched to new conditions. Together the five pages move from a single protein to a candidate molecule, then to safety checks, trial modeling, and reuse of known drugs.
